title: Gastrointestinal Bleeding
subject: Medicine
summary: Assess the source, severity and cause of GI bleeding, prioritise urgent care, and apply pragmatic investigations and management suitable for low‑resource settings.

sections.p: GI bleeding is any loss of blood from the alimentary tract, visible as hematemesis, melena, hematochezia or occult blood. Diagnosis starts with history, exam and simple tests that are available locally.
b: History of bleeding type, timing, associated pain, medications, alcohol, infections

t.b: Low Hb suggests ongoing or recent bleeding
Elevated INR indicates bleeding risk or liver disease

sections.p: Use the Rockall score (clinical + endoscopic) or the Glasgow-Blatchford score (GBS) to predict rebleeding and mortality. In low‑resource settings, a simple clinical assessment (shock, tachycardia, pallor) guides urgency.

In East Africa, the top causes differ by tract: upper GI bleeding is often peptic ulcer disease, oesophageal varices, or gastritis; lower GI bleeding is frequently amoebic dysentery, schistosomiasis, or HIV‑associated lesions.
b: Lower GI: amoebic colitis, schistosomiasis, HIV enteropathy, haemorrhoids

sections.p: Patients may report vomiting blood, black tarry stools, bright red blood per rectum, or painless rectal bleeding. Associated symptoms include abdominal pain, nausea, or signs of shock.
Prioritise bedside tests and simple labs. When endoscopy is unavailable, use imaging or empirical therapy.
b: Plain abdominal X‑ray – rule out perforation

sections.p: Urgent care is needed for shock, active haematemesis, massive hematochezia, or signs of liver failure. Complications include hypovolaemic shock, anaemia, rebleeding, and infection.
b: Signs of liver failure – jaundice, encephalopathy

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care and monitor closely. In low‑resource settings, use available drugs and transfusion protocols.
b: Treat underlying infections – e.g., metronidazole for amoebiasis

sections.p: After stabilization, investigate for chronic causes, counsel on diet, alcohol, and medication use, and arrange endoscopy or imaging as resources allow.
b: Counselling on safe herbal remedies and alcohol reduction

sections.p: Conditions that mimic GI bleeding include haemorrhoids, anal fissures, and non‑bleeding diarrhoea with occult blood.
b: Inflammatory bowel disease – chronic bleeding, pain, weight loss

sections.p: Low Hb may be due to chronic disease; normal platelets may mask thrombocytopenia in early liver disease; a negative stool occult test does not exclude upper GI bleeding.
b: Coagulation tests may be normal in mild liver disease

whenToSeekHelp: Shock (systolic BP <90 mmHg), active haematemesis or massive hematochezia, signs of liver failure (jaundice, encephalopathy), or any patient with persistent bleeding after initial resuscitation.

faq.q: What is the first step in a patient with suspected upper GI bleeding?
faq.a: Resuscitate with IV fluids and blood if needed, then give a PPI and arrange urgent endoscopy if available.

faq.q: Why is octreotide used for variceal bleeding?
faq.a: It reduces portal pressure and splanchnic blood flow, decreasing variceal bleeding.

faq.q: When can you safely stop a patient’s NSAID?
faq.a: Only after bleeding has stopped and the underlying ulcer has healed or been treated.

exam: A 32‑year‑old man presents with coffee‑ground vomiting and hypotension – what is your first action? — Resuscitate with IV fluids and blood, then give PPI and arrange urgent endoscopy.
A patient with known cirrhosis has bright red rectal bleeding – what is the most likely source? — Oesophageal varices; consider octreotide and band ligation.
A child with fever, abdominal pain and bloody stools – what infection should you suspect in East Africa? — Amoebic dysentery; treat with metronidazole.
You have a patient with melena but normal hemoglobin – what does this suggest? — Ongoing upper GI bleeding; continue monitoring and repeat labs.
A patient on warfarin develops hematochezia – what is the first step? — Stop warfarin, give vitamin K, and correct INR before further intervention.

A patient with massive hematochezia is haemodynamically unstable – what is the next best investigation if endoscopy is unavailable? — Plain abdominal X‑ray to rule out perforation and consider surgical referral.
A patient with chronic H. pylori infection presents with epigastric pain and vomiting blood – what is the treatment of choice? — Eradication therapy plus PPI; avoid NSAIDs.

A patient with suspected GI bleeding has a normal platelet count but is jaundiced – what hidden problem might you miss? — Thrombocytopenia due to splenic sequestration in cirrhosis; repeat count after resuscitation.
